body.text: Prabowo Subianto spoke beside Vladimir Putin in September at the plenary of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok. Commentary in The Jakarta Postread the visit as “putting Russia back into the bebas-aktif mix as a third pole” – bebas-aktif being Indonesia’s “free and active” foreign policy. The same column judged that using Putin to reduce Indonesia’s dependence on Beijing was “sound strategy”.
But this third pole has no grounds, because Russia depends on China itself and has accepted Beijing’s procedure for the South China Sea.

First, Russia is poorly placed to balance China, as a recent Interpreter piece suggested when it observed that engagement with Moscow “does not automatically balance the constraints generated elsewhere”. Furthermore, Russia’s own foreign trade has come to depend heavily on China. According to an estimate published by the Carnegie Endowment in September 2025, “Beijing accounts for more than 30% of Russia’s export revenues and provides over 40% of its imports”. However, Russia’s share on the Chinese side was “just 3% of exports and 5% of imports last year” – that is, in 2024.

Furthermore, the two governments’ joint statement of 4 February 2022, issued before the full-scale invasion, declared that strengthening their cooperation was “neither aimed against third countries nor affected by the changing international environment and circumstantial changes in third countries”. In other words, Moscow and Beijing told third states in advance that their choices would not change Russian–Chinese cooperation.
A Russian partner at Tuna adds sanctions risk and gives Jakarta no protection against China.

Second, Moscow has endorsed Beijing’s procedure for South China Sea disputes. Putin and Xi Jinping signed a joint statement on 20 May 2026 in which they stated that the dispute should be resolved through negotiations and consultations between the states directly involved. They also firmly opposed interference in the dispute by forces from outside the region. China’s foreign ministry, in turn, used the same formula in July, in a reply to fourteen governments marking ten years since the 2016 tribunal ruling. It pledged to settle the disputes “through negotiation and consultation with countries directly concerned”.

Nevertheless, Jakarta refused the demand and kept the rig at work until 19 November. Throughout these months, Zarubezhneft held half of the block, with Harbour Energy as operator. Interestingly, Russia appears neither in the Reuters account of the stand-off nor in a 2023 Interpreter piece on Jakarta’s quiet handling of it, which records that “Premier Oil [renamed Harbour Energy after its 2021 merger with Chrysaor] successfully completed its exploration”. This absence is a sign that Russian ownership gave the field no protection, since Beijing pressed its claim against a block that was already half Russian.

Today, the block is being revived with the same Russian partner in place. In May 2026, Harbour Energy sold its half to Indonesia’s Prime Group, and Zarubezhneft told the deputy energy minister it was ready to resume work in June. Meanwhile, Bloomberg Technoz reported in October 2025 that sanctions imposed on the Russian company after 2022 had kept the partners from a final investment decision by making financing difficult. In addition, on 8 October the British government added Zarubezhneft to its sanctions list as a Russian government-affiliated entity.

A view reported in the South China Morning Post in July held the opposite. On this view, Beijing would probably not put its alignment with Moscow at risk to disrupt “a single offshore energy project”. However, the 2021 stand-off suggests otherwise, since Beijing demanded a halt to the drilling while a Russian state company held half of the block. And if Beijing holds back this time, the reason may well lie in its dispute with the Philippines, which the same report described as Beijing's “existing preoccupation”.

In short, a Russian partner at Tuna adds sanctions risk and gives Jakarta no protection against China. Moreover, Jakarta’s own diplomacy has weakened its position in the North Natuna Sea. Prabowo’s joint statement with Xi in November 2024 recorded a “common understanding on joint development in areas of overlapping claims”. The foreign ministry later denied that this wording meant recognising the nine-dash line.

Before the partners commit further, the government could establish whether the British listing will cut the field off from finance and insurance. It could also ask whether Zarubezhneft’s nominated oil suppliers would pass a sanctions screening. At the same time, a recent Interpreter piece noted that the new foreign minister’s first hearing before Commission I would help clarify “which commitments remain open to review”. That hearing is the place to state on the record that the 2024 joint statement does not cover Tuna.

Radityo Dharmaputra is a lecturer in International Relations at Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya, a PhD candidate at the Johan Skytte Institute of Political Studies, University of Tartu, and currently a Think Visegrad Fellow at the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) in Warsaw.
